newsitem.title: USA: US economy seen growing steadily through 1997.
newsitem.headline: US economy seen growing steadily through 1997.

text.p: Rolling quietly and steadlily along, the economy is expected to grow 2.3 percent this year and next, according to a survey of business economists issued Monday.
The survey of 44 professional forecasters by the National Association of Business Economists also saw inflation, as measured by the Consumer Price Index, rising 2.9 percent this year and next.

"Moderate economic growth and low inflation will continue through 1997 and probably much longer," the group said, adding that "while all business cycles eventually end, almost all 44 economists who responded to the survey expect the economic expansion to continue for the forseeable future."
Economists said they expected the economy in the next five years to generally mirror the past five years. Overall annual growth should average 2.5 percent.
The NABE survey also gave high marks to the Federal Reserve, with some 77 percent expressing the view that monetary policy had been "about right" over the past six months.
Separately, the Conference Board said Monday it expected consumers to boost their holiday spending by 5.5 percent this year.
But this bright spot was tempered by a report that existing home sales fell again in October and further declines were expected in the months ahead.
The average American household will spend $450 on gifts this holiday season, up from $430 last year, according to the Conference Board report.

"This increase, in conjunction with household population growth, will lift the U.S. retail sales over the $45 billion mark -- a 5.5 percent increase over holiday sales last year," the business group said.

"The anticipated rise in holiday spending is consistent with recent economic trends, marked by strong consumer confidence levels, moderate inflationary pressures and continuing wage gains," said Lynn Franco, associate director of the Consumer Research Center.
Sales of existing homes fell in October for the fifth straight month due to a slowing economy, and further declines were expected, the National Association of Realtors said.
Existing home sales fell 1.5 percent in October to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.97 million units from a revised 4.03 million units in September, the group said.
"You will see housing numbers continue to come down," said John Tuccillo, chief economist at the association.
Home sales could slip to about an annual rate of about 3.85 million to 3.9 million units in coming months, he added.

Paul Taylor, senior economist at America's Community Bankers, said that if it continued the buildup in the amount of existing homes waiting to be sold could have a spillover effect and slow sales of new homes.

The performance of the housing sector often predicted overall economic growth, said Peter Kretzmer, senior economist at NationsBanc Capital Markets Inc. If housing cooled, economic growth should remain tepid in the near term, he said.
"It indicates the economy continues to slow and probably points toward continued slow consumer durables spending early next year," said Kretzmer.
